title: TypeScript Basics: Types That Catch Bugs
summary: Add types to your JavaScript so TypeScript can catch mistakes before your code runs: typed functions, object shapes, unions, classes and a multi-file project.
objectives: Explain what TypeScript adds to JavaScript and read type errors
Write functions with typed parameters and return values
Describe objects and arrays with interfaces and type aliases
Use union types and narrowing, including handling null safely
Build classes that hide their data and implement interfaces
Split a project into typed modules with export and import

lessons.title: Labels for your values
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## JavaScript with labels

**TypeScript** is JavaScript with one big extra: you can put a label on a value that says what *kind* of value it is. That label is called a **type**.

```ts
let lives: number = 3;
let playerName: string = "Pixel";
let hasKey: boolean = false;
```

The part after the colon is the type:

- `string` means text, in quotes: `"Pixel"`
- `number` means a number: `3`, `9.5`
- `boolean` means `true` or `false`

### TypeScript checks your work

If a value doesn't match its label, TypeScript tells you **before your code even runs**:

```ts
let lives: number = "three"; // ✗ "three" is text, not a number
```

You'll see a red squiggle under the mistake, and a **⚠ Type error** line in the Console. That's TypeScript saying "this doesn't match the label you gave it." Fix the value (or the label) and the squiggle goes away.

### TypeScript can guess

You don't always need a label. If you write `let score = 10;`, TypeScript sees the `10` and works out that `score` is a number all by itself.

### New words

- **TypeScript**: JavaScript plus types. It's checked first, then runs as normal JavaScript.
- **Type**: what kind of value something is, like `string`, `number` or `boolean`.
- **Type annotation**: the label you write after a colon, like `: number`.
- **Type error**: TypeScript's warning that a value doesn't match its type.
- **boolean**: a value that is only ever `true` or `false`.
lessons.exampleMarkdown:
A game's status bar. Every variable has a type label. Try reading each one out loud: "lives is a number, and it's 3." If one of the values didn't match its label, TypeScript would show:

```
⚠ Type error in main.ts, line 2: Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.
```
lessons.exampleCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <title>Status Bar</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <script type="text/typescript">
      let playerName: string = "Pixel";
      let lives: number = 3;
      let hasKey: boolean = true;

      const bar = document.createElement("p");
      bar.textContent = playerName + " | lives: " + lives + " | key: " + hasKey;
      document.body.append(bar);
    </script>
  </body>
</html>

lessons.title: Types, inference and type errors
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Why TypeScript?

JavaScript is **dynamically typed**: a variable can hold a number now and a string later, and you only find out something's wrong when the code runs (if you're lucky) or when a user hits the bug (if you're not).

**TypeScript** adds **static types**: you (or TypeScript) decide what type each value is, and a checker looks for mismatches *before* anything runs. It's used by most large web projects, and every Angular app is written in it.

```ts
let price: number = 4.5;
price = "free"; // ✗ Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'.
```

### Types disappear when the code runs

Browsers don't run TypeScript. A build tool (Vite, in real projects) **strips the types** and the browser runs the JavaScript that's left. Checking is a separate step, done by the TypeScript compiler (`tsc`) or your editor.

That has a consequence you'll see in the preview: **code with type errors still runs**. TypeScript reports the problem; it doesn't stop you. Your job is to get to zero type errors, because each one is a bug waiting to happen.

### The basic types

| Type | Values |
|---|---|
| `string` | `"hi"`, `'hi'`, `` `hi ${name}` `` |
| `number` | `42`, `-1`, `3.14` (one type for all numbers) |
| `boolean` | `true`, `false` |
| `null`, `undefined` | "no value" |

### Annotations and inference

A **type annotation** is the `: type` you write. But you rarely need one on a variable, because TypeScript uses **type inference**: it works out the type from the value.

```ts
let count = 5;        // inferred: number
const title = "Shop"; // inferred too. Hover over a name in the editor to see its type.
```

Annotate when TypeScript *can't* know (function parameters, empty starting values) or when you want to state your intent so mistakes are caught where they're made.

### Strict mode and `any`

`any` switches type checking off for a value. It's an escape hatch, and it hides bugs. Real projects turn on **strict mode**, which (among other things) refuses to silently treat unknown things as `any`. Codegrove's checker is always strict.

### New words

- **Static typing**: checking types before the code runs, as opposed to **dynamic typing**, where types are only known while it runs.
- **Type annotation**: an explicit type written after a colon, like `let total: number`.
- **Type inference**: TypeScript working out a type from the value or code around it.
- **Type error**: a mismatch the checker found, like a string where a number belongs.
- **tsc** (*TypeScript Compiler*): the tool that type-checks TypeScript and can turn it into JavaScript.
- **Strict mode**: a set of compiler checks that real projects turn on; it catches far more bugs.
- **any**: a type that turns checking off for a value. Avoid it.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: A cart line in TypeScript. `name` and `quantity` are inferred; `unitPrice` is annotated to make the intent clear. If `unitPrice` were set to `"2.50"`, the checker would report `Type 'string' is not assignable to type 'number'` on that line, even though JavaScript would happily multiply `"2.50" * 3` and hide the bug.
lessons.exampleCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <title>Cart Line</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <script type="text/typescript">
      const name = "Lemonade";        // inferred: string
      const quantity = 3;             // inferred: number
      const unitPrice: number = 2.5;  // annotated
      const total: number = unitPrice * quantity;

      const line = document.createElement("p");
      line.textContent = `${quantity} × ${name} = $${total.toFixed(2)}`;
      document.body.append(line);
    </script>
  </body>
</html>

lessons.title: Functions with labels
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Tell TypeScript what goes in and what comes out

A function takes values in (its **parameters**) and can give a value back. In TypeScript you label both.

```ts
function double(n: number): number {
  return n * 2;
}
```

- `n: number` means "the value that comes **in** must be a number."
- `): number` after the brackets means "the value that comes **out** is a number." That's the **return type**.

### Now TypeScript can check every call

```ts
double(4);       // ✓ 8
double("four");  // ✗ "four" is a string, but n needs a number
```

The mistake is caught where you *call* the function, before anything runs.

### Labels are required on parameters

TypeScript can guess the type of `let score = 10`, but it can't guess what someone will pass into a function. So a parameter with no label is a type error: TypeScript says it "implicitly has an 'any' type", which means "I don't know what this is, please tell me."

### New words

- **Parameter**: a name for a value that goes into a function, like `n` in `double(n)`.
- **Argument**: the actual value you pass in when you call it, like `4` in `double(4)`.
- **Return type**: the type of the value a function gives back, written after the brackets.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: A greeting machine. The function promises to take a `string` and give back a `string`. Calling `greet(42)` would be a type error: 42 isn't a string.
lessons.exampleCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <title>Greeting Machine</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <script type="text/typescript">
      function greet(name: string): string {
        return "Hello, " + name + "!";
      }

      const message = document.createElement("p");
      message.textContent = greet("Mochi");
      document.body.append(message);
    </script>
  </body>
</html>

lessons.title: Typed functions
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Functions are where types pay off

Functions are the boundaries in your code: values cross into them and out of them. Typing those boundaries means TypeScript can check **every call**, everywhere.

```ts
function area(width: number, height: number): number {
  return width * height;
}
area(3, "4");   // ✗ Argument of type 'string' is not assignable to parameter of type 'number'.
area(3);        // ✗ Expected 2 arguments, but got 1.
```

### Parameters must be typed

Inference works on values, not on parameters. In strict mode an unannotated parameter is an error: *Parameter 'width' implicitly has an 'any' type*.

### Return types

TypeScript infers return types, but writing them is good practice for anything others will call. It turns "the function accidentally returns the wrong thing" into an error *inside* the function, where the bug is. Use `void` for a function that doesn't return a value.

```ts
function log(message: string): void {
  console.log(message);
}
```

### Optional and default parameters

```ts
function greet(name: string, greeting?: string): string { ... }   // greeting: string | undefined
function levelUp(xp: number, bonus: number = 10): number { ... }  // or just bonus = 10 (inferred)
```

A `?` makes a parameter optional (its type becomes `string | undefined`, so you must handle `undefined`). A **default value** makes it optional *and* gives it a value. Optional parameters go after required ones.

### Arrow functions and function types

```ts
const square = (n: number): number => n * n;

// The type of a function: takes a number, returns a number.
let transform: (n: number) => number = square;
```

### New words

- **Signature**: a function's parameter types and return type, e.g. `(xp: number, bonus?: number) => number`.
- **void**: the return type of a function that doesn't return a value.
- **Optional parameter**: a parameter marked with `?` that can be left out; it's `undefined` when it is.
- **Default parameter**: a parameter with a value to use when it's left out.
- **Function type**: a type that describes a function, like `(n: number) => number`.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: Typed helpers for a game. `title` is optional, `bonus` has a default, and `apply` takes another function as a parameter. Its type, `(n: number) => number`, says exactly what kind of function is allowed.
lessons.exampleCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <title>Game Helpers</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <script type="text/typescript">
      function badge(name: string, title?: string): string {
        return title ? `${title} ${name}` : name;
      }

      const levelUp = (xp: number, bonus: number = 10): number => xp + bonus;

      function apply(value: number, change: (n: number) => number): number {
        return change(value);
      }

      const out = document.createElement("p");
      out.textContent = `${badge("Ava", "Captain")}: ${apply(50, levelUp)} XP`;
      document.body.append(out);
    </script>
  </body>
</html>

lessons.title: Shapes for objects
lessons.exampleMarkdown: A team list. `Player` describes the shape, and `team` is a `Player[]`. If one player had `goals: "lots"`, TypeScript would point right at it.
lessons.exampleCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <title>Team List</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <script type="text/typescript">
      type Player = {
        name: string;
        goals: number;
      };

      const team: Player[] = [
        { name: "Ava", goals: 3 },
        { name: "Leo", goals: 5 },
      ];

      for (const player of team) {
        const line = document.createElement("p");
        line.textContent = player.name + " scored " + player.goals;
        document.body.append(line);
      }
    </script>
  </body>
</html>

lessons.title: Arrays, objects and interfaces
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Typing your data

Most code is about data: lists of things, and objects with properties. TypeScript lets you describe that data once and checks it everywhere it's used.

### Arrays

```ts
const scores: number[] = [12, 40, 7];
const names: Array<string> = ["Ava", "Leo"]; // same thing, different spelling
```

Array methods keep the types: `scores.map((s) => s * 2)` is a `number[]`, and in `names.filter((n) => n.length > 2)` TypeScript knows `n` is a string, without any annotation.

### Object types: type and interface

```ts
interface Item {
  name: string;
  weight: number;
  rarity?: string;      // optional: may be missing (string | undefined)
  readonly id: number;  // can be read, but never reassigned
}
```

`type Item = { ... }` describes the same shape. For object shapes the two are nearly interchangeable; teams usually pick one style. Interfaces read like a contract ("anything that is an `Item` has these members"), which you'll use with classes in lesson 5. `type` can also name things that aren't objects, like `type Id = number | string` (next lesson).

### Excess property checks: typos get caught

```ts
const egg: Item = { id: 3, name: "Egg", weigth: 9 };
// ✗ Object literal may only specify known properties, but 'weigth' does not exist in type 'Item'.
//   Did you mean to write 'weight'?
```

Without the `: Item` annotation, TypeScript would happily infer a type with a `weigth` property, and the typo would turn into a quiet `undefined` somewhere else. **Annotate where data is created**, and mistakes are caught at the source.

### New words

- **Interface**: a named description of an object's shape, written with `interface`.
- **Type alias**: a name for any type, written with `type`.
- **Optional property**: a property marked `?` that may be missing; its type includes `undefined`.
- **readonly**: marks a property that can't be reassigned after the object is created.
- **Excess property check**: TypeScript rejecting unknown properties in an object literal, which catches typos.
- **Generic**: a type that takes another type as a parameter, like `Array<string>`. You'll write your own later.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: A typed playlist. `Song` is an interface with an optional `featuring`. `map`, `filter` and `reduce` all know they're working on `Song`s, so hovering over `s` inside them shows `Song` with no annotation needed.
lessons.exampleCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <title>Playlist</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <script type="text/typescript">
      interface Song {
        readonly id: number;
        title: string;
        seconds: number;
        featuring?: string;
      }

      const playlist: Song[] = [
        { id: 1, title: "Neon Rain", seconds: 185 },
        { id: 2, title: "Paper Planes", seconds: 201, featuring: "Ava" },
        { id: 3, title: "Low Tide", seconds: 174 },
      ];

      const minutes = playlist.reduce((sum, s) => sum + s.seconds, 0) / 60;
      const collabs = playlist.filter((s) => s.featuring !== undefined).map((s) => s.title);

      const out = document.createElement("p");
      out.textContent = `${minutes.toFixed(1)} minutes, collabs: ${collabs.join(", ")}`;
      document.body.append(out);
    </script>
  </body>

lessons.title: This or that
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## One value, a few choices

Sometimes a value can be one thing **or** another. In TypeScript, the bar `|` means "or":

```ts
let answer: string | number = "seven";
answer = 7; // fine: it can be a string or a number
```

A type made with `|` is called a **union**.

### Only these words allowed

A union can also list exact words. This is one of TypeScript's best tricks:

```ts
type Weather = "sunny" | "rainy" | "snowy";

let today: Weather = "sunny";  // ✓
today = "snowey";              // ✗ typo! TypeScript catches it
today = "windy";               // ✗ not on the list
```

The word `type` gives your union a name, so you can use it again and again. Now a typo can't sneak in, and when you type `today = "` the editor even suggests the allowed words.

### Adding a new choice

Want `"windy"` to be allowed? Add it to the list: `"sunny" | "rainy" | "snowy" | "windy"`. Every place that uses `Weather` now accepts it.

### New words

- **Union**: a type that allows one of several types or values, joined by `|`.
- **Literal type**: an exact value used as a type, like `"sunny"` or `3`.
- **type** (keyword): gives a type a name, like `type Weather = …`.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: A traffic light. `Light` only allows three words, so `light = "purple"` would be a type error. Try reading the union out loud: "red **or** yellow **or** green".
lessons.exampleCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <title>Traffic Light</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <script type="text/typescript">
      type Light = "red" | "yellow" | "green";

      function message(light: Light): string {
        if (light === "red") return "🔴 Stop";
        if (light === "yellow") return "🟡 Slow down";
        return "🟢 Go";
      }

      const lights: Light[] = ["red", "yellow", "green"];
      for (const light of lights) {
        const line = document.createElement("p");
        line.textContent = message(light);
        document.body.append(line);
      }
    </script>
  </body>
</html>

lessons.title: Unions, narrowing and null
lessons.exampleMarkdown: A loader status as a discriminated union. Inside each `case`, TypeScript knows exactly which properties exist: `result.message` only compiles in the `"error"` branch. The `never` line proves every status is handled.
lessons.exampleCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <title>Load Status</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <script type="text/typescript">
      type Result =
        | { status: "loading" }
        | { status: "ready"; items: string[] }
        | { status: "error"; message: string };

      function describe(result: Result): string {
        switch (result.status) {
          case "loading":
            return "⏳ Loading…";
          case "ready":
            return `✅ ${result.items.length} items: ${result.items.join(", ")}`;
          case "error":
            return `❌ ${result.message}`;
          default: {
            const unhandled: never = result;
            return unhandled;
          }
        }
      }

      const results: Result[] = [
        { status: "loading" },
        { status: "ready", items: ["apples", "pears"] },
        { status: "error", message: "The server is napping" },
      ];
      for (const r of results) {
        const p = document.createElement("p");
        p.textContent = describe(r);
        document.body.append(p);
      }
    </script>
  </body>
</html>

lessons.exampleMarkdown: A `Thermostat` with a private temperature. Outside code can read `reading` (a getter) and call `set`, but `set` refuses anything outside the safe range. Writing `heater.celsius = 99` would be a type error: *Property 'celsius' is private*.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <title>Thermostat</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <script type="text/typescript">
      interface Device {
        readonly name: string;
        readonly reading: string;
      }

      class Thermostat implements Device {
        private celsius = 20;

        constructor(readonly name: string) {}

        set(value: number): boolean {
          if (value < 10 || value > 30) return false;
          this.celsius = value;
          return true;
        }

        get reading(): string {
          return `${this.name}: ${this.celsius}°C`;
        }
      }

      const heater = new Thermostat("Living room");
      const tooHot = heater.set(99);
      heater.set(22);

      const p = document.createElement("p");
      p.textContent = `${heater.reading} (99°C refused: ${!tooHot})`;
      document.body.append(p);
    </script>
  </body>
</html>

lessons.title: Project: Monster card deck
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Your first TypeScript project

Real projects are split into several **files**, each with one job. Your monster card game has three:

| File | Its job |
|---|---|
| `types.ts` | describes what a card looks like |
| `cards.ts` | holds the deck of cards |
| `main.ts` | shows the cards on the page |

### Sharing between files: export and import

Things in one file are private to that file. To share something, put `export` in front of it. Another file can then bring it in with `import`:

```ts
// types.ts
export interface Card { name: string; power: number; }

// cards.ts
import type { Card } from "./types";
export const deck: Card[] = [ … ];
```

`import type` means "I only need this as a label." The `./` means "a file in the same folder."

### Everything you've learned, together

This project uses all of it: types like `string` and `number`, a word list (`"fire" | "water" | "leaf"`), an interface for the card shape, and typed functions. TypeScript checks every file, and even checks that the files fit together.

### New words

- **Module**: a file that shares things with `export` and uses other files' things with `import`.
- **export**: makes something in a file available to other files.
- **import**: brings in something another file exported.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: One file can't show imports, so here is the whole idea in one place: a `Card` type, a typed deck, and a function that finds the strongest card. In the challenge, these pieces live in three separate files.

<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <title>Card Deck</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <script type="text/typescript">
      type Kind = "fire" | "water" | "leaf";
      interface Card {
        name: string;
        kind: Kind;
        power: number;
      }

      const deck: Card[] = [
        { name: "Sparkfin", kind: "water", power: 4 },
        { name: "Cinderclaw", kind: "fire", power: 8 },
      ];

      for (const card of deck) {
        const p = document.createElement("p");
        p.textContent = `${card.name}: ${card.kind}, power ${card.power}`;
        document.body.append(p);
      }
    </script>
  </body>
</html>

lessons.title: Project: Quest log
lessons.learnMarkdown:
## Putting it together

This project is laid out like a real TypeScript codebase: types in one module, logic in a class, and the UI in the entry file. You'll also meet **generics**, the last big idea in this course.

| File | Its job |
|---|---|
| `types.ts` | the `Status` union and the `Quest` interface |
| `QuestLog.ts` | a class that owns the quests and the rules for changing them |
| `main.ts` | creates the log and draws the board |

### Modules and import type

Every file is a **module**: nothing leaves it unless it's exported. `import type { Quest } from "./types"` imports something only used as a type. It's removed completely when the code runs, which makes the intent clear and keeps build tools fast.

### Generics

You've already used generic types: `Quest[]` is `Array<Quest>`, and `document.querySelector<HTMLDivElement>("#board")` returns `HTMLDivElement | null`. A **generic** function takes a **type parameter** (by convention `T`) so it works for many types while keeping full type information:

```ts
function firstOr<T>(items: readonly T[], fallback: T): T {
  return items.length > 0 ? items[0] : fallback;
}

firstOr([3, 1, 2], 0);         // T is number, returns number
firstOr(["a", "b"], "none");   // T is string, returns string
```

Without the generic you'd write `any` and lose checking. With it, TypeScript **infers** `T` from the arguments and the return type follows.

### readonly arrays

`readonly Quest[]` lets callers read an array but not `push`, `splice` or reassign items. The quest log hands out `readonly Quest[]`, so the only way to change quests is through the class's methods (encapsulation again).

### How real projects check types

A real project has a **tsconfig.json** holding compiler options like `"strict": true`. Teams run `tsc --noEmit` (check only, don't output files) in their build pipeline, so code with type errors can't be merged. Codegrove runs the same strict checks every time your preview updates.

### New words

- **Module**: a file with its own scope that shares things through `export` and `import`.
- **import type**: an import used only for types; it's erased when the code runs.
- **Generic**: a function, class or type that takes a type as a parameter, like `Array<T>`.
- **Type parameter**: the placeholder type in a generic, usually written `T`.
- **tsconfig.json**: the file that holds a TypeScript project's compiler options.
lessons.exampleMarkdown: A generic `pickRandom<T>`: one function that works for a list of strings, numbers or objects. Hover-style comments show the type TypeScript infers for each call.
lessons.exampleCode:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
  <head>
    <title>Generics</title>
  </head>
  <body>
    <script type="text/typescript">
      function pickRandom<T>(items: readonly T[]): T | undefined {
        return items[Math.floor(Math.random() * items.length)];
      }

      interface Snack {
        name: string;
        crunchy: boolean;
      }

      const word = pickRandom(["fizz", "buzz", "bop"]);          // string | undefined
      const roll = pickRandom([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6]);               // number | undefined
      const snack = pickRandom<Snack>([{ name: "Chips", crunchy: true }]); // Snack | undefined

      const p = document.createElement("p");
      p.textContent = `${word} · rolled ${roll} · ${snack?.name}`;
      document.body.append(p);
    </script>
  </body>
</html>
